summary:
Ohio stands under the United States national framework on identity documents. Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker, so new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents; passports already bearing an X remain valid until expiry. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad, and litigation on behalf of seven plaintiffs is pending against the State Department.

Entry screening carries its own exposure. A February 2025 State Department rule bars trans athletes from entering the United States to compete in women's sports and flags visa applicants with an internal marking; applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex may be treated as committing fraud and permanently barred. TSA checkpoint procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy. Since March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, have adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and other governments have issued advisories on identity-document and data rules.

Ohio's own facility restriction is the state measure a visitor is most likely to encounter. Governor Mike DeWine signed Senate Bill 104, the Protect All Students Act, on 27 November 2024; it took effect on 25 February 2025, ninety days after signing. The statute requires every public and private K-12 school, college and university in Ohio to designate restrooms, locker rooms, changing rooms, shower rooms and overnight accommodations for the exclusive use of one sex, with users required to match the facilities to the sex recorded on their birth certificate.

Care is constrained for visitors who need it. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," and some hospitals paused care in response; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed full records of patients under 19 from more than 20 hospitals. Specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline were shut down in July 2025, October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, and gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons applies policies mandating conversion-therapy measures for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy, while the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In immigration detention, transgender men have reported forced-labour programmes with beatings and solitary confinement for refusals, alongside reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.
tangentialFactors:
A July 2026 national legal risk assessment published by Erin In The Morning grades every state's legal risk under anti-trans law. Ohio is placed in the worst tier alongside Alabama, Arkansas, Iowa, Indiana, Louisiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, North Dakota, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Utah, West Virginia and Wyoming, one level below the four states marked Do Not Travel: Florida, Idaho, Kansas and Texas. Idaho entered that tier after a felony bathroom ban carrying up to five years' imprisonment, partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists, and Kansas after a civil-suit regime allowing private bounties.

Ohio's law sits inside a wider facilities pattern. A national tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's restriction.

Document rules elsewhere have tightened further. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups describe it as a template for other states, with further bills pending. Foreign governments have treated these trends as a travel issue, issuing advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules.
localsOnly:
Senate Bill 104 applies to educational institutions across Ohio rather than to public facilities generally: it governs K-12 schools, colleges and universities, public and private alike, and designates restrooms, locker rooms, changing rooms, shower rooms and overnight accommodations by sex. Facilities are assigned on the basis of sex assigned at or near birth, and students are required to use the designation matching their birth certificate.

The bill's sponsor was Republican state senator Jerry Cirino. Governor Mike DeWine signed it on 27 November 2024 out of public view and over the objections of Democrats, teachers' unions and civil rights groups; it carries an effective date of 25 February 2025 and contains no enforcement mechanism. The measure is widely known as the state's bathroom bill, while its official title is the Protect All Students Act.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not source Ohio-specific rules on changing sex markers on birth certificates or driver's licences, on hate-crime or anti-discrimination coverage for transgender people, or on adult gender-affirming care restrictions; those questions remain unresolved here rather than answered in the negative.

Whether any complaint, disciplinary action or prosecution has followed Senate Bill 104 since it took effect is not sourced, notwithstanding the statute's absence of an enforcement mechanism.

The tier assignments and state counts come from a single advocacy risk assessment published in July 2026 and from one facilities tally; no independent or official grading of Ohio is in the inventory.

Ohio-specific enforcement practice at airport checkpoints, and how the federal passport and visa rules have been applied to travellers entering or transiting Ohio, are not sourced at state level.
